Reference

Shortwave Radio Glossary

55 shortwave radio terms in plain English, from SINPO and SSB to the grey line and MUF.

A-index
A daily average of geomagnetic activity derived from the K-index; lower values mean steadier conditions.

Active Antenna
A compact antenna with a built-in amplifier.

AM (Amplitude Modulation)
The mode most shortwave broadcasters use: audio varies the strength of a carrier signal.

Balun and Unun
Transformers that match an antenna to a feed line; a 9:1 unun is common for longwires.

Bandwidth (IF Filter)
The width of the slice of spectrum a receiver lets through; narrower cuts interference, wider sounds better.

BFO (Beat Frequency Oscillator)
A receiver oscillator that reinserts a carrier so SSB and Morse code become readable.

Broadcast Season (A and B)
The two shortwave scheduling periods each year: A (summer, from late March) and B (winter, from late October).

CIRAF Zones and Target Areas
Numbered geographic zones used to describe where a shortwave broadcast is aimed.

CW (Morse Code)
Continuous wave: on/off keying of a carrier, used to send Morse code.

Dipole Antenna
A wire antenna cut into two equal halves, fed in the centre; resonant on a chosen frequency.

DRM (Digital Radio Mondiale)
A digital broadcasting standard for shortwave, mediumwave and longwave that gives near-FM audio quality.

DSP Radio
A receiver that demodulates and filters signals digitally, often on a single chip.

DX / DXing
Hearing distant or hard-to-receive stations; DXing is the hobby of chasing them.

Dynamic Range and Overload
A receiver's ability to handle strong and weak signals at the same time without distortion.

EIBI
A free, regularly updated database of world shortwave broadcast schedules.

Fading
Rises and falls in signal strength caused by changing ionospheric paths.

Grey Line (Gray Line)
The band around the Earth where it is sunrise or sunset, often bringing unusually good long-distance reception.

Ground Wave
A signal that travels along the Earth's surface, giving short-range coverage.

HFCC
The High Frequency Coordination Conference, where broadcasters coordinate shortwave frequency use each season.

Ionosphere
The electrically charged upper atmosphere (about 60–1000 km up) that bends shortwave signals back to Earth.

Jamming
Deliberate interference transmitted to block reception of a station.

K-index
A 0–9 scale of geomagnetic disturbance over the past three hours; lower is better for shortwave.

kHz and MHz
Units of frequency: 1 MHz = 1,000 kHz. Shortwave schedules usually give frequencies in kHz.

Longwire (Random Wire) Antenna
A single length of wire connected to a receiver's antenna input; the simplest outdoor antenna.

Loop Antenna
A wire loop antenna, often compact, that can reduce local noise and null interference by rotating.

LUF (Lowest Usable Frequency)
The lowest frequency usable on a path before ionospheric absorption makes signals too weak.

Meter Band
A named shortwave broadcast band, such as 31 m (9.4–9.9 MHz), identified by its approximate wavelength.

MUF (Maximum Usable Frequency)
The highest frequency that the ionosphere will return to Earth on a given path at a given time.

Numbers Station
A shortwave station that broadcasts strings of numbers, letters or tones, widely believed to carry coded messages to agents.

Pirate Radio
Unlicensed broadcasters, often hobbyists, usually heard on weekend evenings.

Propagation
How radio signals travel from transmitter to receiver, including reflection from the ionosphere.

QSL Card
A card or letter from a station confirming that you heard its broadcast.

Reception Report
A listener's report to a station describing what was heard, when and how well.

Relay Station
A transmitter site that rebroadcasts another country's or organisation's programmes closer to the target area.

RFI (Radio Frequency Interference)
Electrical noise from household devices that drowns out weak shortwave signals.

RTTY and Digital Modes
Text and data modes such as radioteletype, decoded with software from the receiver's audio.

SDR (Software-Defined Radio)
A receiver that digitises a wide slice of spectrum and does the rest in computer software.

Selectivity
How well a receiver separates a wanted station from others on nearby frequencies.

Sensitivity
How weak a signal a receiver can detect, usually given in microvolts (µV).

Shortwave (HF)
Radio frequencies from about 3 to 30 MHz (the HF range), which can travel thousands of kilometres by bouncing off the ionosphere.

SINPO
A five-figure code that rates Signal, Interference, Noise, Propagation and Overall quality from 1 to 5.

Skip Zone
The area between ground-wave range and the first skywave landing point, where a signal cannot be heard.

Skywave
A signal that reaches the receiver after being refracted back to Earth by the ionosphere.

Solar Flux Index (SFI)
A daily measure of the Sun's radio output at 10.7 cm, used as a proxy for ionisation and HF conditions.

SSB (Single Sideband)
A mode that transmits only one sideband with no carrier; it needs an SSB-capable receiver.

Sunspot Cycle
The roughly 11-year rise and fall of solar activity that drives long-term shortwave conditions.

SWL (Shortwave Listener)
Someone who listens to shortwave radio without transmitting.

Synchronous Detection
An AM demodulation method that locks to the carrier, reducing fading distortion and adjacent-channel interference.

Time Signal Station
A station that broadcasts precise time ticks and announcements, such as WWV.

Transmitter Power (kW)
The output power of a broadcast transmitter, typically 100–500 kW for major international stations.

Tropical Bands
The 120 m, 90 m and 60 m bands (about 2.3–5.1 MHz), used for domestic broadcasting in tropical regions.

UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)
The world time standard used by every shortwave schedule.

Utility Stations
Non-broadcast shortwave users: aviation, maritime, military, weather fax and similar services.

Waterfall Display
A scrolling spectrum display that shows signals as lines over time.

WebSDR and KiwiSDR
Internet-connected receivers you can tune from a web browser.
